So can I get some evidence for this highly advanced civilization wiped out by the Comet? Other than the planes, helicopters, submarines in hieroglyphs.

You won't get it because there is none. Antarctica has been extremely hostile to human life for millions of years, since before modern humans emerged as a species. There are enough scientific flights and data being collected for climate research down there now that, if there were some kind of major cultural remains deposited in the last 13,000 years, we would have either spotted it directly or found some kind of indirect evidence of it, and that hasn't happened.

Yeah, I don't believe that at all about antarctica. I don't know if there is shit there, but if there was, it would be so easily hidden. We find shit where people actually live all the time. Göbekli Tepe was under a field and wasn't found until a farmer hit a rock or something like that, but he had been growing food on it forever. They keep finding new shit in the amazon all the god damned time. These are places where people are regularly, geogolists study, and we fly over all the time. It would be so much easier to not find shit where people never are.

Both of those locations possess heavy vegetation and have various geological and human activities moving the soil around constantly, which means things get buried over thousands of years and any differences in soil height are smoothed out. Wind, water, worms, rodents, a farmer moving soil around every year with his plow, all of these were happening at Gobekli Tepe and a buried feature was made effectively invisible. Then in the Amazon you have a visibility of about ten meters in most places and the ground surface is obscured by 20 meters of vegetation depth in most places, which renders air observation useless for all but the most large-scale geological features or huge monumental features like pyramids, most of which have already been spotted from the air but not excavated. You can literally walk within 20 meters of a building in the Amazon and never see it.

Meanwhile in Antarctica, you can see directly down onto the ground from aircraft and climate scientists are constantly running flights with very sensitive imaging equipment over swaths of Antarctic territory. On top of that, the ice has been receding since the last glacial maximum which was 13,000 years ago. So this hypothetical civilization would have been built and collapsed when the ice was about as high as it has been since then, which means that any remains of it would be laying on top of the ice sheets and haven't been buried under anything more than snow. On top of that, the cold preserves organic material to a very high degree, so things like collapsed wooden structures would stick out immediately. Ancient buildings are constantly discovered in the desert as the dust and sands shift around because they are easily visible from the air even when buried, burial mechanics are pretty much limited to the wind as not many things or people live out there, and the organic material is well preserved so there's a lot more to find. It's a lot like Antarctica, really.

All of that assumes a civilization is there to be found, which there almost certainly isn't. How would you feed an entire city worth of people in Antarctica even now, let alone during the last glacial maximum? There would only be two methods. One would be to import food. Antarctica is surrounded by the most dangerous waters on the planet and maritime technology was still limited to dugout canoes at the time. Anyone attempting to cross to the Antarctic continent would have almost certainly died. The Southern Ocean claims plenty of lives even with modern technology, and the closest spit of land to Antarctica is Cape Horn, the absolute worst place to be in terms of weather. The name of Cape Horn is synonymous with danger and death, and has been for centuries. Additionally, even if external peoples could move the food to Antarctica, they simply weren't producing enough of it to support an entire civilization; this supposed civilization predates the development of agriculture by a couple thousand years.

The only other method would be through hydroponics or aquaponics combined with a way to substantially increase the temperatures over vast growing areas. I don't think I need to explain why that's unlikely. Both of those growing methods are still fairly experimental today and require intimate knowledge of chemistry and biology to work, combined with the ability to measure things like nutrients-in-solution and adjust them in the right way at the right time.

Could there be a group like the Inuit who survive off a diet of 90% meat and operate as hunter-gatherers? Probably not in Antarctica, because the storms there are much more violent than the storms seen in the north. Every winter would be spent on the knife-edge between life and death as the storms pummeled anyone attempting to live there.

I'm all for alternate historical theories, but the thought of any human life in Antarctica for an extended period of time, let alone an advanced, prosperous civilization, has so much stacked against it that there would have to be a huge deluge of evidence to support it.

So you can speak with such certainty when 10k years ago sea levels were 400 feet lower? We tend to live on coasts. I know when people in my field have spoken with such certainty, they often get made fools of later down the road.

The argument for civilization in antarctica isn't necessarily for the continent as we see it today. There are geographic features around antarctica that are submerged today that were almost certainly islands during the last great ice age. I'm not saying that there absolutely must have been civilization there, but we can't dismiss the idea because out of hand.
